im gonna be real with you if you dont like metroidvanias, platformers, hard games, or are not a patient person this is NOT the game for you. it's difficult and long winded. most enemies do double damage. it's harder than hollow knight by (IMO) a long mile... BUT! it is also one of the most rewarding, gorgeous, fun, fast paced games i've ever played. its art style is beautiful, the soundtrack is a blessing, and there is SO much to discover. this is a game that will keep you occupied for a long time.

and if you're reading this review on steam you're likely playing on pc so if you're struggling you could just mod it with quality of life mods. invincibility, no double damage, weaker enemies, the mods are there to make it easier. its not cheating if it helps you play a game you otherwise cant.

two days ago, i beat silksong 100% on steel soul mode, giving me the steel heart achievement. i feel obligated to write a review just because of how much this game has changed my life. 

tl;dr + spoiler free part: 

this game is stunning. if you like exploring, always finding new things you never would have thought you've learned regardless of how many times you replay the game, if you have time on your hands and don't mind spending it on mastering a beautiful system of combat that makes you feel like you're dancing with your opponents, this game is absolutely for you. 

i do have to warn you, this game is not for people who don't have free time on your hands. this game does not respect your time. if you live a busy schedule and just want to play games for the fun of it, silksong is not that. it is an all-consuming beast that will rot your mind with rage and anger and will likely ragebait you into giving up (similar to rain world, in which i come from.) a perk is that this exposure therapy will make you immune to future ragebait, though!

if you are a busy person and you plan on toughing out silksong regardless, please be patient. there's so much to this game and you will die a lot but it's all so incredibly beautiful. i would highly recommend it to anyone who has the time, patience and curiousity to explore and save a dying kingdom.

when i first got the game back in last year, november, i started out without much combat and platforming experience. yes, i played silksong before i even touched hollow knight (skipped the supposed tutorial for this game, i know). i come from rain world, which is quoted by many to be another similarly difficult game, but in terms of skill i wasn't that good! sure i spent a lot of time playing the game but i had a lot of mods installed that made the game way easier for me.

and trust me! silksong is difficult. it was immensely difficult for me. each boss would take on average 2-3 hours for me to beat. platforming sections would always take me so long to figure out.

[/spoiler]

however feeling the joy of seeing the summit of [spoiler] mount fay [/spoiler] after a 4 hour climb, the satisfaction of being able to aura farm with a push of a button [spoiler] (cross stitch my beloved) [/spoiler], and dancing with the silly butterfly [spoiler] trobbio [/spoiler] ... this game has also made me feel so much, especially the feeling of accomplishment. growing up i could never really have the determination to 'git gud' with video games. but now after more than 500 hours of silksong i understand. in my first playthrough, i was stuck on (act 3 spoilers from now on) [spoiler] skarrsinger karmelita [/spoiler] for days. it genuinely came to a point where i thought it was impossible to beat her, or the [spoiler] abyss climb [/spoiler] , or the dreaded final fight of the game... 

but i toughed it out. i beat [spoiler] karmelita [/spoiler], i did the [spoiler] abyss climb [/spoiler], and i beat [spoiler] lost lace [/spoiler] despite being five hits away from death at any given time and unable to heal. (i used the [spoiler] shaman crest [/spoiler] glass cannon build, because i genuinely wanted to learn the fight without cheesing, and actually beat the game.) so many of the achievements were so nerve-racking - i literally gave up on the speedrunner and [spoiler] twisted child [/spoiler] achievement beacause they were too hard to do, only to convince myself to have another shot at them once i was more experienced, and i went ahead and got them! steel soul was a run where i felt i was riddled with anxiety at every turn. i even had to use a guide run to help me practice the parts of the game that I was the most unfamiliar with. but surprisingly, trusting my gut and just dancing with these bosses carried me such a long way. 

if there's one thing this game has taught me, it's that achievement is possible regardless of how much prior experience you have, and that the route to mastery is tedious and filled with tears and pain. but it works. eventually, as long as you keep coming back for the love of the game, find a breakable wall that you didn't know existed until your 7th playthrough, and find a hidden room you didn't know until your steel heart run, you will just keep getting better and better at the game. you will git gud, just by coming back and refusing to give up.

[h3][i]Hollow Knight: Silksong[/i] | Complete Game Review [/h3] 
(100% In-Game Completion at 60.7 Hours)
[hr][/hr]
I thought [i]Hollow Knight: Silksong[/i] would make me feel like a nimble warrior but in reality, I’m just a very determined pinball.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Compared to [i]Hollow Knight[/i], [i]Silksong[/i] is faster, sharper, and more aggressive, pushing you to stay on the offensive. Hornet’s mobility opens up combat and traversal in a way that feels incredible once mastered, but the game leaves little room for error. Early on, the game can feel difficult and punishing but once it finally clicks, the gameplay becomes one of the most fluid and satisfying systems in the metroidvania space. ★★★★★

[b]Graphics:[/b] Hand-drawn and absolutely dripping with personality. The new world of Pharloom trades the decaying loneliness of Hallownest for something more vibrant yet no less haunting. Every area feels distinct, detailed, and alive in its own strange way. I kept pausing just to take it all in… right before the game reminded me that standing still is a terrible survival strategy. ★★★★★

[b]Sound:[/b] The soundtrack matches the pacing perfectly and adds real weight to both movement and combat. Not every track stuck with me the way the music from [i]Hollow Knight[/i] did, but [i]Silksong[/i] still nails the atmosphere where it counts (pun intended). ★★★★☆

[b]Story:[/b] Just like its predecessor, the narrative is fragmented and intentionally vague. You’re given various goals throughout but the ‘why’ is buried in subtle clues and environmental storytelling. It’s intriguing if you enjoy piecing things together, but if you want a clear, direct narrative, this won’t give it to you. ★★★☆☆

[b]Replayability:[/b] A variety of builds, tools, and hidden paths provide some incentive to return. However, unlike its predecessor, the absence of pathway split-route achievements reduces the drive for meaningfully varied re-runs. Beyond optional challenge playthroughs involving steel soul mode and speed running, its long-term pull feels more limited. ★★☆☆☆

[b]Final Thoughts:[/b] The game refines what made the original great while demanding more from the player in return. [i]Silksong[/i] is faster, tougher, and—in the wise words of Hornet—expects the player to ‘git gud’. Nevertheless, it also feels incredibly rewarding once you start to master the movement and combat mechanics.
[h3]Overall Rating: 8/10, gorgeous, unforgiving, and definitely worth the inevitable suffering. [/h3]

This game is Art - and like all Art, it's not for everybody. Team Cherry has created an uncompromising masterpiece aimed at players who've delved deep into Hollow Knight and enjoyed mastering its combat. These players will likely adore Silksong; the skill ceiling and combat depth are way higher now, both regarding Hornet's moveset and enemy difficulty and complexity. Hornet handles like a dream and requires a higher degree of mastery to keep up with all but the most basic of enemies. This is great for players like me who enjoy the process of "gitting gud" but brings us to why some players won't enjoy the game, quality be damned.

Silksong is hard. Not just that, but punishing as well. This is very deliberate, and feels incredibly rewarding once you overcome what the game throws at you, but it comes at the cost of accessibility. If you play games to chill out and relax, chances are that the frustration factor may be too high for your tastes. Even if you liked Hollow Knight, if what kept you playing was mainly the exploration and atmosphere, and you preferred a more shallow involvement with combat, snubbing the Colosseum and Godhome, Silksong may end up being "too much". A tragedy, given Silksong's excellent worldbuilding and ludonarrative harmony (translation: you'll get to intimately feel the pain of what it means to be an inhabitant of Pharloom).

If you are new to Hollow Knight and Silksong and want to give them a go, I would recommend playing Hollow Knight first. Silksong was designed to give veteran Hollow Knight players the "first time spankings" experience all over again, with all that entails.

Silksong is like a dream that you never want to wake up from. It's easily the best indie game I've ever played. I loved Hollow Knight, but Silksong takes everything that made the original great and elevates it to another level. It feels like an upgrade in every possible way.

This game completely hooked me. No other game has made me want to play this much. While I was playing, it felt like I was living in its world. It's one of those rare experiences that makes you sad when it ends because you know you'll never be able to experience it for the first time again.

I truly believe Silksong deserved to be Game of the Year 2025. Many people ignored it saying it's just another Hollow Knight,but for me it's so much more than that. It's the ultimate GOTY. I've also played expedition 33, which is fantastic in its own right, but it didn't come close to the impact Silksong had on me.

The credits soundtrack was absolutely beautiful. It genuinely made me cry as I reflected on my journey from the very beginning to the end. Few games have ever connected with me on that level.

Silksong is a masterpiece and a perfect 10/10. It's a game that every gamer deserves to experience at least once in their life. Now all I can do is eagerly wait for the dlc and hope it isn't too far away.

[h3][b] Even when the road appears to climb toward the peak, its true destination lies buried deep within the mountain’s darkness [/b][/h3]

After I got the platinum in Hollow Knight, I was waiting for the sequel. And I’m going to say it straight: [b]it was 10/10 experience[/b]. Not because I’m trying to be dramatic, but because [i]this game didn’t just meet my expectations – it blew past em and gave me one of the strongest gaming experiences I’ve had[/i].

Tbh my first time with the game wasn’t what I expected at all. I finished Silksong and thought like "yea, kinda ok," but it didn’t hit me the way HK did. I was honestly a bit disappointed. Then, while watching some random Silksong video, I learned one key thing: what I considered as completin the game was basically only about 50% of what the game actually offers – and not even close to the ending Team Cherry clearly treats as the main one.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3611197693
That instantly hooked me. I got curious and motivated, and decided to beat it properly: go for 100% and grab the platinum (I’m still finishing it up, but I’ve only got a couple achievements left near the end). And after that second, let's say "real" run, everything clicked.

After completing Act 3, this game became not only my favorite in its genre, but one of my favorite games overall. And i put a ridiculous amount of effort into it. Clearing all three acts on Steel Soul was brutally hard af, and I genuinely went through the full range of emotions while doing it. It’s also the first game that made me plug in a controller just to finish Act 3, because the final missions were simply unreal (at least for me, prob skill issue) on keyboard. And still – that’s exactly why it stuck with me. [i]It ended up being one of the best experiences I’ve ever gotten from a game[/i].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3575045376
I expected a lot, seriously. But [i]I didn’t expect my expectations to be exceeded this hard[/i]. And the cool part is that at first I was disappointed, and after the second playthrough I only regretted not doing it in the right way earlier.

One of the biggest wins by TC for me is how [b]the game feels more dynamic while also being bigger[/b]. Combat, playthrough, even just exploring the world – [i]everything feels faster, more alive, and as a result more exciting[/i]. At the release, the difficulty felt like it was intentionally over-the-top(which was frustraitihg as hell tbf), but it got nerfed pretty quickly, and [b]now the game is in a near perfect state[/b]. Yes, [u][i]it’s harder than Hollow Knight[/i][/u] – and for me that’s not a downside. [b]That’s one of its main advantages[/b].

And then there’s the thing that really surprised me: [b]the world and exploration[/b]. If the first game was built almost from nothing, the [i][u]sequel takes the best parts and turns them into something far stronger[/u][/i]. Yeah, it’s subjective, but while Hollow Knight is comforting and pleasant in my memory, the locations and the whole of Pharloom didn’t just impress me – they absolutely floored me. The world design feels unmatched, and the best part is that even near the end of Act 2 I kept finding something new: new areas, new characters, new events, new experiences.
During 3d Act I went through Craw Lake purely out of curiosity and discovered a whole new location with its own story and interesting things happening there. [i]And moments like that happen a lot[/i]. The game actively encourages you to explore – [i]and it’s worth it[/i], because exploration here (mainly) isn’t for the checklist. [i]It actually rewards player's curiosity[/i].

On top of that world sits a [b]constantly gripping atmosphere[/b]. The bar is just as high as in the first game, and it syncs perfectly with everything that’s happening – [i]it boosts tension, highlights key moments, and makes the journey feel more real[/i]. Huge respect to Team Cherry for that – and especially to Christopher Larkin for another incredible and atmospheric soundtrack.

[b]Another improvement[/b] I loved is [b]the way the story is presented[/b]. Hollow Knight feels very Dark Souls-like: you walk in silence, explore, collect lore piece by piece, and do all the work yourself. [u][i]Silksong tells its story in a different way – more like a typical story-driven game[/i][/u] – and because of that, Hornet feels more alive, so does the world. For me, that’s a big plus: [i]it’s not just lore in the background, it’s a more direct connection to what’s going on and you actually understand it[/i].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3570472807
There are cons, but to me they aren’t very noticeable: [b]except for one thing[/b]. [u][i]Some side quests/wishes can feel very repetitive[/i][/u]: find-kill-bring,find-bring, take-deliver, and so on. It’s not something that ruins the game, but at times it does feel like routine. That said, it’s easily outweighed by how many strong moments and advantages the game throws at you along the way till the very end.

So yeah. I expected a lot – but I got more than I was ready for. Silksong is the kind of game that might not hit the way you want on a first run, but if you actually dig into it, push through the acts, commit to exploration, and really finish what the game has to offer – it pays you back with such a level of emotion and reward that you just sit there thinking: Alright. This was something special.

It's very rare for me to write a review, but for Silksong I feel compelled to.

To start, the art is stunning. There are some truly beautiful areas in this game with small attentions to detail that make the world feel more alive. Like the small ants carrying away the bodies of defeated foes. The same, if not better, little particle effects with the grass and bugs in each area. Not to mention the flying bugs that go past after you climb out the starting areas. 

The characters are made with such love; not just visually, but their animations, voice acting and overall design make each character so endearing. You'll fall in love with them, even your fast travel bug has one of the most impactful scenes in the game. From playing dice with a lonely bug in a cave, to battling the beasts of Pharloom side by side with a trusted NPC friend you're going to feel at home in these hostile lands. Not to mention an item you get later that allows you to hear all of the bugs singing. Some of the bugs even sing terribly which is somehow more charming.

The music is breath taking. So many tracks have been so carefully and thouroughly crafted to represent each area. Sometimes you'll wonder (in two specific areas) why the music is so sad, and the more you find out about them, the more you'll realize exactly why it sounds like that. The final final boss (two finals on purpose) has one of the most amazing tracks in the game. I get chills just hearing some of the tracks, let alone that final theme invoking such strong emotions.

Speaking of emotions, the story and lore (which I won't go into for spoiler reasons) is so wonderfully portrayed. With some moments that made my cry outright and moments of peak joy and wonder when you piece it all together.

The traversal in Pharloom vastly outmatches anything in any other metroidvania style game I've played, there's always somewhere else to go if you're struggling. There are hidden paths to get to your objectives that are so mindblowingly considered for, it makes the kingdom of Pharloom feel like a living, breathing place. The platforming is brutally difficult on a first playthrough especially but so rewarding. 

The bosses are mindblowing, very often I'd say to myself, "There's no way they can top this boss." Only for the next boss to somehow be even more amazing. You'll never tire of the spectacle.

With all this glaze, it's time to talk about difficulty. I'm on the fence here. On the one hand, I personally do not mind the difficulty but I also understand that some people want to just chill on their couch and unwind after a stressful work day and not want to bash their head against a wall. So if you're not ready for what feels like the fight of your life at times, with some truly brutal run backs and such. Then I'd say it's probably not the game for you. However this is a game that challenges you but also, there's always somewhere else to go that will make what you're struggling with. A new tool or weapon upgrade, sometimes a utility tool that makes the situation easier. 

When it comes to the difficulty: Team Cherry was very particular in how they crafted the encounters, I wouldn't want the game to play any other way. Each enemy, boss and obstacle is teaching you how to play better. It'd be like if I tried to play guitar and got frustrated it still sounded bad after a few weeks. Skill at a new game takes time. It won't be for everyone but I think it's worth it. I do think the game would benefit from having accessibility features like Celeste, where they're actively discouraged but do exist for those to just see where the game goes. But that may ruin the intent behind the design so maybe the "art" is more important here.

All this being said, the game is a steal at the price tag. 
I hope you enjoy your journey in Pharloom everyone!

Silksong does what Hollow Knight did well way better, and some things it did badly worse.

Positives:

• Fantastic art design on just about everything, far more varied than Hollow Knight and full of little details.
• Very satisfying and varied platforming. While there isn't a full on White Palace/ Path of Pain section, similarly challenging platforming bursts are weaved throughout the game.
• The crests, Silk skills and tools offer great gameplay variety.
• Very well designed world packed with NPCs.
• Enjoyable questing system although it does accentuate the backtracking and back & forth aspects which I don't like very much but it is nowhere near as bad as Hollow Knight.
• Intuitive world design. In Hollow Knight, if you are playing without a guide, it is incredibly easy to get lost for hours on end, trying to find the next upgrade. So much needless backtracking and padding because of that. Not a problem in Silksong.

Mixed:
• The soundtrack is great BUT tracks are on average shorter than Hollow Knight's. Not sure why the composer chose to go with that direction but I'm hoping it'll change for the updates/ DLC.

Negatives:
• Near every negative in Silksong can be chalked up to what I call excessive TCT - Team Cherry Trolling™. It is there on every step of the way whereas in HK such moments would be a little less frequent: 
- Traps/ even more enemies after already arduous platforming or fighting sections, you don't get a single break really.
- Bosses that have arenas with debilitating effects (like Maggots, preventing healing), no platforms to stand on at all, add spam DURING boss fights and whole Colosseum-like gauntlets before you can even fight the actual bosses. Other bosses that'd be finely designed, have some extreme visual clutter (Trobbio) or otherwise poorly visible attacks (Lost Lace).
- Extremely and I mean incessantly annoying flying enemy design, I do not understand what they were thinking when they made enemies that fly away from you constantly, input read your jumps and movement direction for their projectiles and freak around like they are on meth.
- Cumbersome design = difficulty, apparently. The lack of QoL is very real. I do not understand why Team Cherry still think not displaying your position on the map or withholding the ability to autocollect resources that drop from enemies, basic game features present in like every other game, should be locked behind equipables? Why don't maps update in real time as well? Just unnecessary padding.
• A negative that isn't specific to Team Cherry as it is present in other 2D games as well, it is however handled horribly in both Hollow Knight games: contact damage. In most other games that have CD, you have to misplay really badly and find yourself inside the enemy to be damaged. Or it could be the version of contact damage I actually like, where it is only active around whatever enemies/ bosses use as a weapon. In Hollow Knight and Silksong on the other hand, touching any single pixel of any enemy or boss at any time will immediately hurt you, sometimes even for 2 Masks worth of damage. You do not pair a system like that with enemies that move erratically and love to jump/ teleport on you, it cheapened the difficulty in HK, Silksong is no different in that regard.

All in all Silksong is an amazing game that is well worth your time when the experience isn't being dragged down by Team Cherry's juvenile trolling attempts, that I honestly thought they'd grow out of considering they were working on Silksong for near a decade, but nope, if anything they got worse with it. I've been playing Fromsoft games since Demon's Souls and have played pretty much every Soulslike there is out there as well so I have quite a bit of patience when it comes to petty trolling, only the most egregious instances get a reaction out of me but I can imagine how infuriating it would be for others that aren't used to stuff like this, so I absolutely understand the negative reviews and those that ended up dropping the game because such sections/ moments do make Silksong feel like a chore to play, especially throughout Act 3. However if you have the patience to overcome the nonsense, I can't recommend the game enough. Or just mod it out!

"This is like when the smug kid (you actually want to hate) is indeed the best in class". I never jived with Team Cherry's silent treatment during Silksong's development, to the point I didn't even buy the game for a good while, but now that I've played it... man, this is a total masterpiece, it surpasses the original Hollow Knight (and that was the best metroidvania ever at the time) and it is maybe matched only by Nine Sols in recent years. Silksong is a crazily big, dense and rich game, and it's also polished to near perfection.

Everyone's favourite bug in red, Hornet, is captured by strange bugs and finds herself in the kingdom of Pharloom, drawn to the citadel high above the land to understand who wanted to kidnap her and why. It's a setup with just the right intrigue to give you a clear objective throughout, but also vague enough that you're free to just go nuts. Much like HK, the storytelling in Silksong is actually super interesting. You're basically witnessing the death throes (maybe) of another kingdom, but you learn more about its history and its structure by multiple sources: dialogues (many NPCs this time around), bestiary entries, collectibles, and just the environments themselves, which actually could be playing the biggest part. The story you get out of it is tragic, dark, incredibly captivating and not too esoteric to understand. The sense of history the game world has is unparalleled in the genre, better than the first HK (and it was one of its selling points even back then IMO); the same is true for the world design and its impeccable sense of geography. Pharloom is a fantasy bug kingdom alright, but it feels rich, complete, believable, one of gaming's most exciting worlds. Plus, Hornet is great as a protagonist, she has a personality which is expressed in different ways and she's a total and utter badass. I loved playing as her.

The gameplay has familiar foundations, but many improvements. It's metroidvania perfected. Combat is snappy, fluid, fun. Hornet has incredible agility and almost all of the traversal abilities can be incorporated into combat. You have different Crests, classes of sort that alter your basic needle moveset and some core abilities, and also have different notches to equip tools. Tools are an evolution of HK's charms and come in three colors, with red being akin to the Castlevania subweapons. Add into the mix some Silk Skills that act as HK's spells and you have an incredibly rich, flexible and customizable setup. You could have different Crests for bosses and exploration, or hone on your one favourite and master that. Up to you. The exploration is similarly incredible. Pharloom is nonsensically large, and there are a ton of areas to explore, each completely unique and each brimming with countless secret passages, setpieces, collectibles, subtle stories to tell. The sense of wonder and discovery is one of the game's biggest strengths for me, and the basic game loop that comes from it is intoxicating. Even when the game doesn't reward you with something tangible (like a new tool), you can almost always find something unique and strange.

Now, something about difficulty. I don't know if the game's difficulty has been significantly patched since launch, but I just can't see the problems people talk about. Silksong is a hard game for sure, but it always keeps a sort of openness. Most tricky situations have unconventional solutions that reward exploring (High Halls gauntlet? You have two NPCs that can help and you can permanently disable an enemy type. Bilewater boss runback? There's a hidden bench to find. Etc.). Also, you have so many options to tackle a boss or an arena. I've seen that many people really hated the arenas, especially before bosses, and it's true they're way more common in this game but I found them fine? Like, instead of a boss fight, I saw those instances as a mix of different challenges and I found them very stimulating. Then again, I might not be a good average case for this. I've played tons of metroidvanias and had 100% completion in Silksong in 36 hours, which is way below the average. So I don't know, it was a tough game, but always completely fair and never frustrating for me. Zero. Nada.

Artistically and musically, this has few rivals. The art style is immaculate and so full of unnecessary details that bring the world to life. Animations are painstakingly crafted, the visual theming is so strong. The artists at TC are savants, and the same can be said about maestro Christopher Larkin for having crafted - once again - one of the best soundtracks of all times. There are SO MANY incredible tracks here, and the contribution of the music to the mood and atmosphere can NOT be overstated. It clicks all the pieces together.

Overall yeah, I am FUMING to say this, but Team Cherry did go above and beyond and did craft a complete masterpiece. Just don't be quietly smug about it next time, eh?

Hollow Knight Silksong is a step above the original Hollow Knight in many ways, but in my opinion, the thing that Silksong does best is it's platforming and movement. In a world of metroidvanias that often recycle the same methods of movement, Silksong innovates by changing the world you explore and how you interact with it. The world is focused on wall climbing, becoming a core mechanic early on and being extraordinarily helpful, considering Silksong's focus on verticality. Platforming with the harpoon is a dream, the dash feels great, and no part of my kit went neglected. The game constructs areas for you to use and learn your new abilities, making you commit them to memory. Eventually these inputs become second nature, and you're moving Hornet in flourishing and beautiful ways that make you (truthfully) feel more skilled than you actually are. 
As much as I had to say about the movement, there is an unfortunate downside. The game is too dark. This may sound like a trivial complaint, but more often than not, for large portions of Act 2 you are exploring areas that don't encourage movement. Across act 2 you are presented with endless ways to get around, sure. However, when a good bit of these places to explore are either enclosed areas or platforming puzzles where you can only see in a two foot radius around Hornet because of said darkness. While one can argue a lot of these darker/enclosed areas are optional, a statement in which I agree, I don't think that's a valid criticism. If presented with an opportunity to explore and upgrade, you'd be foolish not to, especially considering the difficulty of the overall game. Making these secrets and areas that often times rely on platforming with INCREDIBLY reduced visibility and maneuverability, makes the experience unfun. A general rule of thumb with Silksong is that reward rarely meets effort. If there is a potential platforming puzzle well out of your way, you'll most likely be treated with a handful of rosaries or shards. However, if a random breakable wall you missed has a challenging gauntlet of buzzsaws and traps you'd never see until you've already died on them- those are your moneymakers. Your mask shards, spool fragments, etc. To upgrade in this game, you have to suffer, and in most cases, really put up with a lot of challenges I would consider unfair. It really disturbs the overall beautiful flow of the platforming that Team Cherry found.
Visually, this game is amazing. Each area carries its own distinct atmosphere between music and visual identity. Platforming makes sense in these areas- in universe, the objects you to and fro from don't stand out in any particularly offensive ways, and usually add to the world, which I personally think is a very impressive feat. Inflating balloons to hop on, bells to ring and bounce from, traps on the walls of sketchy areas- all of these examples and more establish a beautiful world that I almost didn't want to leave. After I completed Silksong, I revisited Hollow Knight to compare the games, as I'm sure a lot of people did. It is, and I say this truthfully, just how much the art improved between these two games. The difference between animations, personality, and world is very visible. Hollow Knight was already a world that was very alive, but Silksong improved without overdoing, and has wormed its way into one of my favorite settings.
There is bad to this world however. Nothing immersion breaking, but a complaint I couldn't help but think about. Hollow Knight had fewer areas, however, these area's were important. Each bit was connected to the story in meaningful and insightful ways. Silksong, sadly, doesn't commit to this. There are areas like The Sands Of Karak or Deep Docks that grow and change as the story continues, however, there are also areas like Wisp Thicket or Wormways. While being interesting areas that work well as setpieces, they have very little to offer in terms of actual reason. Wisp Thicket is a random area that holds an effigy to a god. That's it. Wormways just... Has worms in it. Things occur there later, but nothing that warrants the area really existing at all. To me, these aspects are very shallow and underthought, making them stand out in aways that don't always feel great.
It's time that I officially talk on the biggest complaint I've seen about Silksong; the double damage. Contrary to what I said earlier, I do not have a big problem with the double damage. The game introduces it in a way that makes sense. Fire hurts more than a normal attack. You go to Deep Docks, see that the game is choosing to escalate in difficulty, and that's it. Hornet's 3 mask container heal is enough to deal with this, as well as her air heal, which puts an emphasis on understanding opponents before finding your room to make a move. Opponents who deal double damage are often built on skill, and the game rewards you handling them. You are supposed to pick your battles, and the game is sure that you know it.
There are aspects to the double damage debate that I do want to bring up however. Firstly, they make upgrades feel minor. Increasing your health often feels like a waste of time.  If you reach an even number of hearts, you've gained no reward. What problem is this if the double damage makes sense? Well, sadly, the double damage really doesn't always make sense. An enemy half my size that I've been seeing since the game started doesn't need to deal 2 masks of damage and I say that with full confidence. Once you make it to act 2 and on, the game gives up on dealing only single mask damage. it's double damage from there on out. Working with Hornet's limited health pool you get steamrolled. You'll get mad, but it's still WORKABLE. At points though, I found myself fed up with tanky enemies that dealt 2 masks of damage, and at those points, I found myself diving into spikes or other hazards to avoid them, because taking 1 mask from a hazard was better than dying. That should never be the case in a game like this, where the fights are supposed to be challenging and meaningful, not dragging and annoying. Then you get to a point when all enemies deal 2 contact damage on top of their two mask attacks, and the game loses a lot of the 'challenge' and begins to be hard for the sake of being hard. 
I have one final ending point I'd like to go over before wrapping this review up. The final boss of the game. This was frustrating for me, and I must admit, it did not feel like it was through much fault of my own. The final boss has a handful of attacks, but any and all attacks from the first phase are the main culprits to this conversation. Without spoilers, they have about 3 or 4 separate attacks, all telegraphed relatively well so you know what you're expecting for the first half of the attack. The second half of the attack is RNG based from what I can tell. Sure, they may be using the charge attack, but instead of finishing the charge, they could randomly hop in the air and dive back down on you. There is no indicator of this, and all of these attacks have at least 3-4 variations that are randomly picked. It was this that kept me stonewalled at this fight. It was not fun to be randomly deciding how I should try to avoid an attack that may not come at all. Sadly, this is the only time the game does something like this, and it's at the very end. It left a bad taste in my mouth, and I hope that Sea of Sorrows takes time to go over this with a fine tooth comb.
Silksong is an amazing game. Sadly, it's not better than Hollow Knight in my opinion. A more potent story didn't make up for the faults I had with the gameplay. However it's an experience I wouldn't trade for anything despite the faults. That's the beauty of this game though. Everyone's playstyle is so different, that they all struggle and succeed in different ways. I've never had a more adaptable gameplay experience, and I encourage you to try it for yourself before trusting my opinions over your experience.

[h1] An Outlier [/h1]
In a time were most new releases are either $100 CAD with micro transactions, filled with bugs, or have horrible performance, this game feels like a breath of fresh air.

There had been nearly no information about Hollow Knight's sequel for many years. Then they just drop this thing for 25 bucks. It's bigger and better than the critically acclaimed first game. It's extremely polished, looks great, movement feels better than any other games like it... It's just... A very very clean experience.

[h1] The game they wanted to make [/h1]
One thing that surprised me about the game - And I honestly don't know how to say it any other way - is this disregard of game design "best practices".

We see more and more AAA developers tooting their own horn about how great their UI & UX are, how sleek and streamlined their gaming experience is etc. There seems to be this obsession with simplifying games, removing friction and maximizing dopamine.

And I feel like there are many things in Silksong that are not things you would see in modern games, like a boss with a longer / tougher runback for instance. But not even necessarily with regards to difficulty or convenience. It just feels like they stayed in their corner and made what they wanted to make exactly the way they wanted to make it, without trying to please everyone, which results in a very cohesive experience.

[h1] Exploration [/h1]
Few games have given me the same feeling Dark Souls 1 has. And you may jump to the obvious conclusion that I'm talking about difficulty but it's not about that at all.

One of the aspects I appreciate the most about both games is how vast the world feels. And it might sound strange, considering there are a ton of open-world games out there with larger maps. It's about how it [i]feels[/i].

If I could sum up that feeling, I would say that whenever you [i]think[/i] you've seen all of it, there's more. You start off having no sense of the game's depth and the more you play, the more you think to yourself "There's [b]another[/b] whole area here? What??". I'm sure (or at least I hope) you've had that feeling before.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The character is an absolute treat to control.

I like exploring in HK but it could feel a bit slow at times. Silksong feels [i]fast[/i]. It feels [i]snappy[/i]. I love it.

Gradually unlocking new methods of moving around is really exciting and by the end of the game you're zooming everywhere and feel in perfect control of the character, it feels incredible.

If you've seen anything of the game, you might think it's all about the bosses. And while bosses are indeed a big part of the experience, I think I appreciated the [b]platforming[/b] aspects just as much. I'm a big fan of platformers and I honestly miss them. And this game has [b]such[/b] good platforming sequences. The kinds where you're jumping, dashing, bouncing, double-jumping, dashing again, wall jumping... It feels awesome to pull off.

There is a degree of customization with combat. I'm honestly a bit boring and just did the whole game with the default setup but you do unlock quite a few options throughout the game, which I know quite a few people appreciate.

[h1] Bosses [/h1]
The bosses are obviously the big highlight and a big part of what the game is about.

The game is faster and quite a bit tougher than Hollow Knight in general. So even the very first boss will likely be a challenge to most people.

And listen. It's a specific kind of game. You need a specific kind of mindset going into it.

It's going to take you time to truly get it, to really appreciate it. You're going to fail a lot. But it's through failing that you improve until you prevail. And I promise that once you do, the satisfaction you'll have will be proportional to how tough it was to get through it.

You will feel completely hopeless against some of the bosses.

You will die within seconds of the fight starting and think you've finally met your match. That you won't be able to progress past that point. You know the fight is probably a lot longer than what you've seen, but have no sense of how long it is because there are no health bars.

You might get frustrated. Think that it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, that the runback is long and annoying and unnecessary.

But then it clicks. You enter this flow state. You start improving, getting further in the fight each attempt. You stop thinking about beating the boss and start enjoying participating in the dance, learning each attack and finding a way to avoid it, react to it. Even when you die, you start appreciating the brief moment of respite you get as you make your way back to the boss. You take a deep breath, push through the frustration of failing and transcend it. You embody the spirit of an immortal warrior that is destined to battle for eternity, be it futile or fruitful. Losing is no longer an option, because there is no such thing as losing. It's just part of the process.

Then you make it.

And you press forward.

[h1] Story [/h1]
This is one of those games where the story is a bit abstract and lets you piece things out without overexplaining everything. How much you're willing to invest yourself into it is entirely up to you. Just know that you're not really missing out on anything if you're not remembering every single little detail.

I'm the type to take things in as they are and just enjoy the ride, without digging too much about lore. Much like FromSoftware's games, I love the atmosphere in general and everything feels immersive, credible and well-pieced together, even if much of it ends up going over my head.

I appreciated the dialogues and cutscenes nonetheless!

[h1] Is it too hard? [/h1]
There are a few aspects that I found frustrating at first but that I eventually just learned to accept as part of the experience. It's something that I thought about a lot and I think that it's specifically those frustrating experiences that make the game, moment to moment, that much more memorable. The most vivid memories I have of games I played when I was younger are typically the biggest challenges I was able to surmount.

It's a tricky balance. Would giving me more health, having fewer / shorter runbacks, more benches, taking less damage each hit, lowering bosses health etc. have made me appreciate the game more? At some point I might have said yes. After going through it... I don't think so. I don't think I would change anything about the difficulty.

Whether you're willing to put up with it is ultimately up to you. But know that it's not a relaxing game where you sit back and enjoy pretty visuals. It's meant to be challenging to people who beat the first Hollow Knight, so it's definitely going to be extra challenging for anyone not familiar with the genre or who do not usually play more difficult games.

But I sincerely don't think it's [i]too[/i] hard or unfair. I think anyone can do it. It really is only a matter of patience and perseverance. If you absolutely cannot stand the idea of retrying an area or a boss 10-20 times, or if you hate having to take a break and trying again the next day because you can't beat a boss... Then you probably won't have a great time.

If you're on the edge about it... I [i]strongly[/i] encourage you to try and change your mindset. You [b]absolutely[/b] can do it. You just have to keep going at it and you'll make it the whole way through with great satisfaction. I sincerely think it's worth it.

[h1] Hollow Knight: Silksong [/h1]

I am reviewing this game based on my own personal experience and taste. [b]At the end of this review, I'll also provide some important tips and guidance for playing Silksong to help you on your journey[/b]. So, this is both a review and a guide!

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Given the previous game, player expectations for the gameplay are incredibly high. However, it's clear that the gameplay and mechanics this game puts in the player's hands are incredibly varied and unique.
Silksong's build system and Crests help you progress according to your own playstyle, allowing you to create your own personal build. The diverse abilities you acquire over time and through progression make the gameplay significantly smoother and more engaging.
Silksong map is considerably larger than Hollow Knight's, and you'll encounter many different environments and enemies. You'll face over 300 different types of species in this game, which shows its sheer scale.
The quests you encounter can be engaging at times, but some can be tedious and boring, and the main purpose of these quests is to reach Act 3 and, consequently, the true ending of the game. Silksong is divided into 3 Acts. Act 3 actually appears based on your choices in completing certain quests and the final boss of Act 2, and it's in this act that the true ending and the entire story the player has been seeking unfolds.
To prevent the game from becoming repetitive, Team Cherry has designed specific mechanics and systems for each act. For example, the travel system in Acts 1 and 2, as well as how you purchase maps, is different, introducing the player to a new way of interacting with the environment. Also, in Act 3, you'll get a new ability for reaching travel stations that is really fun and cool.
The platforming in this game is so flawless and special that it needs no explanation.
[b]Overall, the gameplay and mechanics, aside from a few minor bugs, are outstanding.[/b]

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story of the Hollow Knight series is one of my personal favorites, and in my opinion, few games in this genre have such a deep and beautiful narrative. In Silksong, because Hornet can actually converse with NPCs, the storytelling process is incredibly endearing and understandable.
However, unlike the first game which had a more direct narrative path, in Silksong you have to explore and investigate more to follow the story. Of course, this very thing makes players more curious to continue.
Silksong's cutscenes are thoroughly exciting and cinematic, getting you hyped to keep playing. The story also answers questions from the previous game and serves as its complement.
[b]Be sure to play Act 3 to fully understand the story and get the true ending.[/b]

[h3]Graphics and Art Style[/h3]
Overall, the graphics and visual effects of the Hollow Knight series are incredibly creative and captivating, and Silksong is even better than its predecessor, leaving nothing to be desired. The thematic design of the different map areas, enemies, and bosses is executed perfectly.
[b]In short, this game has a beautiful and delightful art style.[/b]

[h3]Soundtrack[/h3]
I have immense respect for Christopher Larkin for composing the soundtracks for the Hollow Knight series, and I congratulate him on creating such masterpieces. The soundtracks in some map areas are very calming and enjoyable (like Bilewater, Cogwork Core, Bone Bottom, ...) and are perfectly matched to the theme of that area.
The soundtracks for some bosses are incredibly unique and exciting, filling the player with tension.
[b]In my opinion, the soundtracks of the first Hollow Knight is on another level, but also Silksong's soundtracks has its own charms, and we should be grateful to Christopher Larkin.[/b]

[h2]Some ​Negative Points (Common Player Feedback)[/h2]

​It's necessary to mention some of the negative points that players have pointed out:

1. ​Excessive damage from simple enemies, which makes the beginning of the game more difficult and frustrating for players. Some basic enemies can take 2 mask shards from you!

2. ​Long and tedious runbacks to bosses waste a lot of time. The best solution is to always rest at the closest bench to the boss.

​3. Unnecessary challenges for some upgrades and quests, like upgrading Hornet's needle. You have to find pieces of "Pale Oil," and for the last 2 upgrades, you face very difficult challenges. For the final upgrade, you must find all the Fleas in Pharloom and then complete all the Flea-Festival challenges, which takes a lot of time.

​4. The extreme difficulty of some bosses and arena fights when you face them without upgrades. You can finish the game without getting the double jump ability and many other skills. In this state, you might face some bosses with low equipment and weak builds, which will give you a very hard time.
I strongly recommend having a suitable build and, as much as possible, getting upgrades, Mask Shards, and Spool Fragments before facing bosses. Silksong is designed so that as you upgrade yourself (most importantly, leveling up your needle) and gain different abilities, the bosses become easier. They only seem extremely hard at the beginning.
One of the arena fights I faced very early and without good equipment was the one in the top left part of the Citadel (High Halls), and I spent a lot of time trying to beat it. Worse yet, if you want to speedrun the game, this arena fight is a truly difficult challenge.

​[h2]Tips and Guidance[/h2]

​I highly recommend that you finish the game on your own for the first time so you don't get spoiled on this amazing game and can have a pleasant experience with the story. But for your second playthrough or subsequent ones, I recommend the following tips:

1. ​For a checklist of things you've found, bosses you've beaten, quests you've completed, or anything else, you can use the following app. It's extremely helpful in this regard, allowing you to have a cleaner map and progress in a more organized way:
[url=https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sefir.den.ogmhksilk]​OGM: Map for HK Silksong[/url]

​2. Make sure to buy (unlock) the game's benches and travel stations as much as possible to have closer checkpoints to the bosses. Also, a tip you might already know from the first Hollow Knight is that you can quit to the main menu and reload your save to return to your last checkpoint (the last bench you sat on or the last location where you received an ability or Crest). This is useful for shortening your path or preventing death and the loss of your rosaries. (Of course, whether you like this method or not depends entirely on your playstyle.) For me, just walking through the Silksong map was enjoyable enough that I didn't need to do this, but it became extremely necessary for finishing the game on Steel Soul mode.

3. ​Each Crest has its own specific gameplay and mechanics, and you should choose one based on your playstyle. For me, the [u]'Wanderer'[/u] Crest (I recommend getting this early on after getting the Cling Grip ability) and the [u]'Architect'[/u] Crest were very good.
equipping a few good tools will help you immensely during the game. I recommend using the [u]'Cogfly'[/u] tool along with [u]'Pollip Pouch'[/u]. This combination is very helpful. Also, use the [u]'Warding Bell'[/u] to protect yourself while healing.

In the end, I have to tell you that you are facing an incredible game and you are going to have a wonderful experience with it. Silksong is highly optimized and also has a low price compared to other games. This game is really worth your time.

There really isn't much on this game that I can say that hasn't been said already, with that being said I'm going to praise every single aspect of this game.

Hollow Knight: Silksong is what every sequel should strive to be. It expands on quite literally every aspect of the original game in such unique and interesting ways that allows it to have its own identity while still having all the core aspects of what make Hollow Knight well, Hollow Knight.

Take the tool system for instance. It's this games twist on the charm system from the original, separating them into three types. Red tools which are combative weapons to attack the enemy with, blue tools which help in combat with effects like a longer needle or extra healing, and yellow tools which are there to assist with exploration. It's such a simple change from the original system yet it adds new layers of depth with the builds you're able to make and massively changes how you play the game depending on what you equip.

This game is absolutely massive too. Hollow Knight had 19 distinct areas to it, each and every one of them feeling distinct with their own unique identities, enemies, bosses, puzzle, and items to pick up. Silksong on the other hand has 32 UNIQUE AREAS. That's just the size though, every area is squirming with things to discover, secret rooms, relics, new tools, skills, it just goes on and on. Speaking of bosses, the bosses in this game are a step up from the ones in Hollow Knight. Beating Steel Soul in Silksong feels less like finishing a game and more like surviving an ordeal you’ll remember forever.

This mode takes everything Silksong already does: precision platforming, brutal bosses, and tight combat. It removes your safety net. One death and it’s over. No excuses. No “just one more try.” Every room becomes a risk assessment. Every heal is a decision. Every new enemy makes your palms sweat.

What really shines in Steel Soul is how well the game supports mastery. Enemy patterns are readable but punishing. Bosses demand calm, not mashing buttons. By the end, you’re not stronger because of your upgrades. You’re stronger because you got better. When I finally cleared the last stretch without dying, I had to just sit there for a minute and breathe.

Exploration feels different too. In normal mode you wander. In Steel Soul, you plan. Do you detour for resources and risk an unfamiliar area, or play it safe and fight underpowered? That tension is constant, and it’s intoxicating.

Is it stressful? Absolutely. I lost a run deep into act 2 (you'll see which boss I mean). Considered calling it there. But really the magic is just that: Steel Soul turns Silksong into a personal challenge, not just a metroidvania. When you win, it feels earned in the purest sense.

If you’re the kind of player who loves high stakes, clean mechanics, and the quiet satisfaction of overcoming something genuinely hard, Steel Soul alone makes Silksong legendary.

Let me start with the obvious: [b]Silksong is an excellent game.[/b]

I spent dozens of hours exploring Pharloom, fighting bosses, uncovering secrets, and pushing through some extremely demanding encounters. Team Cherry once again delivered a huge, ambitious metroidvania that will probably remain a reference for years. But I also think the game is being treated as if it were flawless, and I strongly disagree with that assessment.

[h2]What Silksong Does Right[/h2]

[list]
[*]The world is huge and packed with content.
[*]Hornet's mobility is fantastic.
[*]Several bosses are among the best Team Cherry has ever designed.
[*]The Act III twist is genuinely excellent.
[*]Exploration remains addictive from beginning to end.
[*]The overall production quality is remarkable for an indie game.
[/list]

Had this review only been based on content quantity, ambition, and production value, it would be an easy recommendation.

Unfortunately, I believe some core design decisions hold the game back.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Boss Design: Harder Is Not Always Better[/h2]

Silksong often feels more difficult than Hollow Knight.

The problem is that it does not always feel difficult for the right reasons.

Several bosses rely on:

[list]
[*]Extremely fast attacks with limited telegraphing.
[*]Attacks dealing 2 masks of damage.
[*]Sudden repositioning or teleportation.
[*]Anti-air options that leave very little reaction time.
[*]Enemies or hazards appearing directly on the player.
[/list]

Yes, these encounters can be learned.

Yes, they can be mastered.

But mastering something does not automatically make it good design.

As someone who defeated Nightmare King Grimm, Pure Vessel, Absolute Radiance and completed Pantheon 5, my issue is not difficulty itself.

My issue is that Hollow Knight's best bosses usually felt fair.

Silksong's hardest bosses often feel punitive first and fair second.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Progression Feels Weaker[/h2]

One thing Hollow Knight did exceptionally well was making every major upgrade feel transformative.

In Silksong, I rarely experienced that feeling.

I became stronger.

I unlocked new tools.

But I rarely felt that my relationship with the world fundamentally changed.

The sense of growth never reached the same level as Hollow Knight.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Crests Are Disappointing[/h2]

This may be my most subjective criticism.

I simply never found the crest system particularly interesting.

Many crests feel like minor adjustments rather than meaningful playstyle changes.

Compared to the charm system from Hollow Knight, the result feels less impactful and less memorable.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Soundtrack Lacks Standout Moments[/h2]

This was perhaps my biggest disappointment.

Hollow Knight gave us unforgettable themes.

Years later, I can still hear City of Tears, Greenpath, Sealed Vessel, Grimm, or Hornet in my head.

After finishing Silksong, I struggle to recall a single track that left the same impression.

The music is good.

But for me, very little of it is memorable.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Characters and Story[/h2]

This is where the gap with Hollow Knight becomes the most visible.

The original game gave us characters like Quirrel, Cloth, Elderbug or the Last Stag.

Silksong introduces many characters, but very few left a lasting impression on me.

Sherma and Shakra stood out.

Most others felt surprisingly flat, including some characters that seemed positioned to play a much larger emotional role.

The story is not bad.

But unlike Hollow Knight, I found myself caring more about the next boss than the next narrative revelation.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Silksong is bigger.

Silksong is harder.

Silksong is more ambitious.

But I am not convinced it is better.

Hollow Knight felt meticulously polished in almost every aspect.

Silksong often feels like a brilliant game that reached further, but not always with the same level of refinement.

I absolutely understand why many players will call it a masterpiece.

I simply think it is a masterpiece with very real flaws.

First and foremost, following up on the masterpiece that is Hollow Knight was never an easy task and the overwhelming hype that surrounded this game with its silkposts and neverending memes made this release somewhat of a climax of 2025. However, despite my hesitation going in I can safely say that despite some minor flaws, Silksong is another defining masterpiece from Team Cherry that will stand the test of time.. 

For context, I have finished the game on all endings and did most of the achievements, all in all 80 hours of gameplay. I did not touch steel soul so I can not comment on all the extras added through that route but I have heard it did spice up the game with more secrets and added characters. I did take my time exploring all the nooks and crannies in this quite enormous world and never once did I feel like I got enough of this games gorgeous and remarkable worldbuilding that both expands on the lore from Hollow Knight, but also carves itself a brand new niche in the story of the fallen realm of Pharloom. To give this a fair rundown I have ordered my humble opinions in an internet-friendly structured list.

[h3]The great [/h3]
[list]
[*]The worldbuilding of Team Cherry is the stuff of legends. The various areas and their interconnected stories make for a sublime journey through a realm of twisted nightmare and horrible beauty. Travelling through Pharloom and its delicate handcrafted environments is an amazing experience and despite the sheer scale of it all you never feel lost or confused. Each area has its specific enemies and tells a different story about the fall of the empire and how its inhabitants struggled to survive the aftermath. 
[*]The overall gameplay is sublime in its excellent and precise combat and movement and I really love how different Hornet handles versus The Knight. In the beginning it took a bit getting used to but the end result of the tools combined with the variation in crests were perfect and I truly enjoyed feeling the combat being just right during some of the bosses and challenges.
[*]The crests that give you your attack pattern are diverse and varied, and even though I ended up using the standard crest most of the game, the diversity and intricate differences are a brilliant way of seasoning the already excellent gameplay. 
[*]The bosses were great, each telling a different story and fighting perfectly into its domain. In the end I faced them all and had a great time challenging my own lack of reaction.
[*]The music is bloody great. Simply perfection! 
[/list]

[h3]The not equally great [/h3]
[list]
[*]The many arenas where you are swarmed by a ton of regular dudes felt alright at start but quickly turned into a chore. I get it, we need some breakpoints to try out our skills and an arena where you throw in a couple of enemies can be great, unless they get too regular. Not a great annoyance, but quite remarkable in its “mundanity” compared to the great bosses!
[/list]

[h3]The improvements to be made (IMHO) [/h3]
[list]
[*]The extra “layer” of currency. Now you have to juggle Silk (soul equivalent), Shards and Rosaries, each filling a certain niche that quickly made me fall back into a weird grindy loop that felt awful. The Silk powers your abilities and heals you, but if you, like me, need to heal a lot, this is what you will invest the majority of Silk into. I have heard arguments for the fact that using certain abilities speeds up encounters, but since most of them are just technical dances you really do not need the speed, only the health for these misjudged dodges and strikes… Shards are used in some quests/wishes and to recharge your tools, something you tend to need to do a lot if you keep bouncing off bosses. Early game you will drown in shards, late game, not so much. Rosaries are my main gripe since they are not dropped by all the enemies, yet are used to unlock benches, fasttravel, gadgets and much much more. Did it really need to be so many different currencies? And do you really want to use those fancy tools knowing you will run out of gas if you fail too frequently? To me this felt poorly executed and ended up being a grind, something that actually might be highly thematic in this dystopian bug-riddled fantasy.
[/list]

How would you rate a game, where 80% are awesome and 20% make you question the sanity of its creators? There's a saying that if you put a spoon of ♥♥♥♥ into a barrel of honey, you will end up with a barrel of ♥♥♥♥. This is how I feel about Silksong.

It has very high highs and extremely low lows. It's a masterpiece in world building, the level design to some extent, the atmosphere and environmental storytelling are great. Unfortunately, all of it is ruined by game design decisions, which just make the game straight unfun.

The main issue is that game does not respect your time, and overstays its welcome if you decide to 100% it. In act 2 I installed the teleport mod (and it was the only change I made to the game), because I was just tired of running around the same areas dozens of times. I get it that it's a metroidvania, and you're supposed to explore and do multiple runs of the same areas, but backtracking is really pushed into the unfun zone, especially if you're not following any guides and try to figure everything out on your own. This could have been mitigated by more generous fast travel system, like, porting to benches, or at least having a build in teleport in the game.

Second issue, and it's a big one, is how the game tries to make you feel. It raised a lot of discussions in the media regarding what makes the game fun, where lies that boundary where game's challenges are to its detriment. There was one video which made a good point, IMO, that we rarely mind the games which are difficult, but not punishing (e.g. Elden Ring), or the games that are relatively easy, but very punishing (most roguelites). Issue with Silksong is that it's both difficult and punishing. Dying is very real, happens often, and the progress setback can be tremendous.

A lot of game design decisions are aimed at forcing you in a constant state of anxiety, where you are afraid of losing your progress and resources. Platforming sections can go for a long time without checkpoints, and death can set you a few minutes back. Bosses have notoriously long runbacks, and often require you to clear a gauntlet before you can even fight them. Your tools use a resource which is not replenished after death. All of this puts a real weight on you to stay alive, and it's not a game where you can one-shot all encounters just by being cautious. A lot of platforming sections and bossfights require you to gradually learn and progress them. 

The idea here is that the more you build the anxiety up, the better it will feel when you finally overcome challenge or reach safety. Problem is that I don't feel anything apart from relief. I kill a boss and my only thought is: thank god I don't have to do it again. The game annoys you more than it makes you feel good.

There are also smaller game design decisions that just make you annoyed or frustrated. The design of flying enemies, for example. They always try to stay out of your melee range, either doing ranged attacks from the corner of the screen, or just sweeping across with a melee attacks immediately moving out of your range. It can be fun trying to figure the tactics out when you fight them for the first time, but you encounter them just so much and so often that dealing them becomes annoying simply because of how much time they waste.

The fact that TC loves to put flying enemies in gauntlets or in the middle of the bossfights does not help either. A lot of encounters end up very chaotic, and you're practically forced to tool dump if you want to keep your sanity, and it puts even more weight on you to stay alive. I think, there's a universal agreement that double bossfights don't work unless boss movesets are fully synchronized, or AI is built in a way that it's unlikely that you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥ by overlapping attacks. TC made masterclass double bossfight in their previous game (Mantis Lords) and some good ones as well (God Eater, Watcher Knights), it's incomprehensible to me how they managed to drop the ball in Silksong so spectacularly. There are a lot of fights where you're not methodically learning the complex movesets, you're just trying to survive the chaos and clutch victory by some luck, without really feeling that you even deserved it. You're just glad its over.

IMO, the main issue of the game is that Team Cherry worked in isolation for so long. They had no outside input, they did not know whom are they balancing the game for, and they ended up making a very niche product which caters either to people who were very good at the original game (speedrunners, pantheon players), or to people who can't have fun without high stakes and anxiety.

Well first thing first I enjoy the game immensely for few reasons:
1) The art direction is exceptional, from the music and sound design to the background art.
2) The levels are very fun if you like high-octane 2D action games like Dead Cells or 2D platformers like Rayman Origins or Legends.
3) There is huge build variety that even influences on Hornet movesets which encourage multiple playthrough to try different items or crests.
4) Hornet is super fun to control and move around. I definitely prefer her to the knight in the first game.
5) Most of the bosses feel like real skill checks, which I prefer. This is something that can't be said of the first game, where most bosses felt like random enemies with high HP bars. The enemy variety and density also makes each new zone unique and fun to discover. 

That's where the positives end. Now, on to the criticism. It seems like Team Cherry has a major issue by confusing difficulty with lack of quality of life. 
1) I don't understand why we still have to waste a slot just to see where we are in the map. 
2) there are way too many secrets. And worst of all, many of them lock game content, such as biomes or bosses. Some even lock progression to more game endings. Other Metroidvanias have an item that you can unlock at the end which hints at a secret when you enter a room.
3)While tolerance may vary from person to person, I find that there are too many gauntlet rooms. It doesn't help that most Silksong enemies are not only fast but also register your inputs just to walk, fly, or dash away from your attacks.
This brings me to my next point about runbacks. A handful of bosses are not only locked behind a runback, but also behind waves of enemies. Nine Sols has bosses that are as hard as or harder than those in this game, but the runbacks are super short. In many difficult precision platformers and boss rush games, you respawn immediately after dying. It makes the experience more enjoyable and encourages you to Git Gud.

In short, the game hides a lot of content behind secrets. It's also an endurance test because you have to go through the same long obstacles multiple times to improve. In my opinion, the game actively discourages players from progressing just for the sake of "difficulty." Team Cherry allows this because their loyal fanbase will defend their unfriendly design decisions. If another development team wanted to design a mechanically challenging game without considering quality of life or accessibility, I bet their game would be criticized and ignored.
Oh, and 99% of the quests are boring, yet you need them to progress. Rather than balancing the game's pacing with peaks and valleys, the developers included quests similar to those in Power Washing Simulator to slow down the high-octane action. These are the same kinds of quests that were criticized in MMOs, gacha games, and poorly received Nintendo games.

Now that you know the caveats, hopefully you'll enjoy the game!

Hollow Knight: Silksong is a sequel that I had frankly a lot of expectations for, and if I am honest… This game exceeded all the expectations I had.

[b]Story-wise[/b], one thing I instantly noticed is how much more present the story feels during gameplay. While I’m not entirely sure how to explain it, but the best way I can describe it is that it feels like you always have a certain goal in mind, and that goal constantly shifts as you progress. Now, this is a goal largely set by yourself, so it can be quite personal, but I personally felt like I always had some idea of what I was searching for or what I was working towards. It made the story feel more integrated into the actual gameplay than it did in Hollow Knight. Hornet also feels much more alive as a protagonist. Obviously, a large part of this comes from the fact that she actually speaks, unlike the Knight, but I think there is more to it than that. 

[b]Atmosphere-wise[/b], I think Silksong stands just as tall as Hollow Knight, if not slightly higher. The locations throughout Pharloom feel much more alive, which creates a noticeable contrast with Hollow Knight. In that game, Hallownest was intentionally designed as a fallen and decaying kingdom, so much of its atmosphere revolved around ruin, isolation, and the remnants of a world that had already collapsed. Pharloom, by comparison, feels far more active and inhabited, giving its environments a greater sense of vitality. Detailed background lighting, sharper animations, and a more dynamic audio design all contribute to this. Traversing through Pharloom feels more reactive. These elements make the environments feel more like living spaces that exist independently of the player that it did in Hollow Knight. Personally, I prefer the atmosphere of Silksong over the original, but I think this ultimately comes down to personal preference. The two games are clearly going for different atmospheric identities: Hollow Knight embraces a melancholic, decaying world, while Silksong leans more toward something vibrant, animated, and constantly in motion yet still quite melancholic.

[b]Gameplay-wise[/b], Silksong is a massive step above Hollow Knight for me. Hollow Knight already has incredibly satisfying movement, but the Knight generally feels more grounded. His movement is deliberate, and while abilities such as Mantis Claw, Monarch Wings, and Crystal Dash give him considerable mobility, they often feel more like tools for navigating the world than direct extensions of his combat style. Hornet, by comparison, feels as though her entire moveset has been designed around movement and momentum.
One of the biggest additions in Silksong is the Tool system, which feels far more active and gameplay-focused than Hollow Knight’s Charms. In Hollow Knight, Charms primarily modify the Knight’s existing abilities, affecting things such as damage, spell efficiency, movement, or healing. Tools, by comparison, feel much more like actual pieces of equipment that you actively incorporate into your gameplay. Rather than simply altering how Hornet’s abilities function, they can give her entirely new ways to attack, defend herself, or interact with enemies.
What I particularly appreciate about Tools is how much more connected they make preparation to your actual playstyle. A Tool isn’t simply a passive bonus that you equip and then forget about. Many of them provide abilities that you can deliberately activate during combat, effectively making your equipment another component of your moveset. This creates a much greater distinction between different playstyles, because changing your Tools can fundamentally alter how you approach an encounter rather than simply making the same strategy slightly more effective.
Another particularly interesting addition is the Crest system. Crests essentially function as different loadouts that can fundamentally change the way Hornet plays. Rather than simply providing passive bonuses like Charms, different Crests can alter aspects of her moveset, attacks, and overall combat style.
Then there are Silk Skills. These are special abilities that give Hornet additional ways to utilize her silk during combat. What makes them particularly interesting is how distinct they are from one another, giving you a variety of active abilities that you can incorporate into your playstyle.
Now all I said is mostly scratching the surface of the difference in gameplay and I truly think that gameplay wise, this game is miles better than Hollow Knight

Overall, Hollow Knight: Silksong takes everything that made the original special and expands upon it in meaningful ways. Its story feels more integrated into the gameplay, giving Hornet a stronger sense of purpose as she moves through Pharloom. The atmosphere is just as impressive, trading Hallownest’s decaying isolation for a more vibrant, active, and living world without losing the melancholic ton. Most importantly, the gameplay feels like a major evolution, with Hornet’s movement, Tools, Crests, and Silk Skills creating far more depth and freedom in both exploration and combat.
While Hollow Knight remains an incredible game, Silksong feels like a genuine step forward rather than simply a bigger version of its predecessor. After all the expectations surrounding it, the fact that it managed to exceed mine is genuinely impressive. If you enjoyed Hollow Knight or simply love challenging Metroidvania games, [b]Hollow Knight: Silksong is a must-buy[/b].

There's genuine stuff to like here, so let's start with that.
Visually this game is stunning. There's a variety of regions, each with their own look and feel, and the art direction is just incredible. Some areas feel reminiscent of the first game alongside completely new environments, and both work really well. Enemy designs look great, the visual effects are clean, and the whole aesthetic meets the bar the first game set.
The world also feels more alive this time. There are a lot of entertaining NPCs, and the addition of proper questlines makes interacting with them enjoyable if you want to fully immerse yourself in the world, though they don't always feel worth doing.
The gameplay takes some time to ramp up, but when you reach that flow state after unlocking more abilities, it feels great. Silksong builds on the first game's moveset through the introduction of Crests, alongside expanded movement options. It makes movement faster and allows for levels of skill expression.
The boss fights are a lot of fun for the most part, there's a good range of them and some are genuinely great. That's kind of where my positives end though, and that's the frustrating part.

The most straightforward way I can put it is that a lot of Silksong feels designed to be annoying first and challenging second.
Enemies hit considerably harder than feels fair (with double mask damage) right from the start while your own damage feels very underpowered, basic enemies take too long to kill, and the world is densely packed with them. Staggering enemies is also practically non-existent, so unless you dodge in time you're almost guaranteed to get hit from a lunge attack.
Getting around makes everything worse. The game is more linear than its predecessor, so when you don't know where you're going you end up grinding through the same areas while you try to figure it out. Exploration feels unrewarding more often than not, and if you're not heading in the right direction you've just put yourself through a gruesome journey for nothing.
The region layouts are a pain to navigate, bench placement can be punishing featuring some of the worst runbacks known to man, and the game has a habit of throwing in cheap traps. Bilewater in particular may be one of the most frustrating areas I've played through in any game. It wasn't fun, I wouldn't even call it difficult, it was just tedious in the most unearned way possible.
Then there are the bosses. In isolation a good number of them are solid and some are excellent, but compared to the first game they fall pretty flat. Hollow Knight's best fights had a real sense of grandeur that made certain encounters feel like genuine milestones. Silksong doesn't. The ceiling of what Team Cherry can do is on full display in a handful of late-game encounters from the first game, which just makes the lineup of endgame bosses in Silksong feel like an even bigger missed opportunity.

This game really feels like it's playtime padding with annoying design choices disguised as difficulty. When it works, it really works. The problem is that it doesn't work consistently enough, and the stuff that doesn't is too frequent to overlook.

There is so much damn time wasting in this game. 

Double damage is not a challenge. It's just a waste of time. 

Runbacks are not a challenge. They're just a waste of time.
