It also makes exploration painful. The developers say that if you're having a hard time, explore further. Well, every room is full of flying guys that do homing projectile damage that follow you to the ends of the Earth, and every pit is full of spikes that do two damage. Why explore? It's just more pain, just like everything else in this game. 

Where's the fun here? At some point I just have to call it. Git Gud isn't an adequate retort, it's just a cover for the many oversights the developers made in this game that trapped their pretty and artistically beautiful game underneath a totally ruthless, unfulfilling, and time-wasting experience.

This is the type of game that makes the limitations of Steam's review system apparent - Whether or not I recommend this game depends a lot on who you are as a player and what you like to play. Hard to capture any kind of nuance like that with a simple boolean "yes"/"no" review rating, so I'm settling on asking the question "Would I recommend this game to anyone?" with a thumbs down. The TLDR on why is because most people are going to be turned off by this game's brutal level and enemy design. You can get around this with the help of mods on PC tbf, but the average player isn't going to do that - either because they're not on PC, they lack the technical knowledge, or they're simply just not interested in altering the artist's original vision for the game.

This is coming from someone who calls Metroidvanias and Soulslikes their two favorite genres, who fully completed the original Hollow Knight multiple times and calls it one of their favorite games of all time. I don't mind a difficult game; in fact I cherish them when they're done right. This game is a polished work of art, but one that seems to take sadistic pleasure in it's difficulty, on a level above the first game. Don't get me wrong - the first HK has some of the most challenging bosses and levels I've ever encountered in a game, but crucially this kind of content is off the beaten path and optional (for the most part). The main game was also challenging, but reasonably so, rarely to the point of feeling unfair. Silksong on the other hand regularly feels unfair along the main path; I can't imagine what playing it must be like for a newcomer, but even as a metroidvania/soulslike/HK "vet" I've been struggling to continue with it because of how frequently it just doles out unreasonably challenging sequences for the surrounding level context. It does help that you can take multiple paths, and that everything is so well polished mechanically and with how it's presented - but multiple paths don't do you a ton of good when all of them end with brick walls that you're expected to either hurtle flawlessly or smash into repeatedly.

As a dev myself I can't help but notice all of the little details that add up to paint the picture of what the devs were trying to create, and I can't help but feel like Silksong paints a clear picture of a dev team that spent too long in isolation and relied too little on outsiders for QA/testing. As you develop a game, you tend to lose sight of what that game is like for other people because of how creating it affects your perspective; but also because they tend to get incredibly good at their game (natural result of playing and testing it constantly, for 7 years in this case...). If you don't get people with fresh perspectives to test it enough along the way and you don't iterate enough on that feedback, you risk making a game that pisses people off more than it gives them that satisfying feeling of overcoming a challenge. And to be fair, this stuff is incredibly difficult to get right.

I'll also concede that although I've made it through a lot of the game (seems I'm about halfway through?), I haven't finished it, so this is a "review so far" and I might change it by the time I finish it, or if they manage to patch these problems out and give it a better balance. The world is gorgeous, the characters are full of personality, the toolset Hornet uses is really fun (moreso than the first game in a few ways, I love her agility and mobility for instance), the SFX and music are haunting and beautiful, and all in all you can tell the devs poured their hearts and souls into this game... So it hurts a bit giving it a thumbs down after this long wait, but I feel obligated to warn newcomers with how big the game has become, and I hope that can change over time so I can recommend it more broadly. 

In the meantime, if you love these types of games and don't mind an imposing challenge of an adventure, you'll probably find yourself loving this game and I can give it a thumbs up for it to you in it's current state.

After 68 hours and beating the game at 93% completion, I feel quite confident in my following review:

Silksong *can* be a fun game. The art, the story, the explorable map, the combat. It's all great. But silksong is full of many baffling decisions and a completely different design philosophy from Hollow Knight.

If you really like Hollow Knight enough to have the patience to legitimately complete the true godseeker pantheon: Only then I would recommend you Silksong.
If you otherwise thought that the godseeker pantheon was too hard and too punishing to bother with, that's exactly what awaits for you in silksong.

Silksong is HARD and PUNISHING. I do not say this as a good thing. Hard games can be fun, and so can punishing games. But both combined veer into the territory of extreme tedium and frustration.

I will now point out specific things that I did not like:

- The early game does a poor job at easing you into the game. The game starts hard, to the point that the midgame will feel a lot easier in comparison because its not really all that harder than the very first bosses of the game, except by then you'll have a lot more items and upgrades to suit the situation.
- As a continuation to the previous point, the biggest culprit is the fact that throughout the entire game, everything the player touches will remove 2 masks of health, out of the 5 you start the game with, and you may very well spend your first 10 hours of the game before you collect enough masks shards to upgrade that to 6. At all points in the game, you have half as much health as your health UI would suggest. To the point team cherry has realized they overdid it and have slowly been patching certain enemies and environment hazards to deal only 1 mask of damage, but they're very tentative in their approach, so don't expect patches to eventually fix the early game difficulty more than they've done so far, which in my humble opinion has been far from enough.
- A lot, and I really do mean a lot, more than half of the bosses have incredibly lengthy runbacks. Expect to spend more time running back to the boss than you will spend actually fighting them. And the runbacks get worse and worse as the game goes on, every time you think "God this runback was the worst", you'll be surprised to see theres one even worse a few bosses down the line, with mandatory path-of-pain levels of parkour and multi-round normal enemy guantlets before each attempt. Some of the worst runbacks can take upwards of 4-12 minutes just for the priviledge of one attempt at the boss.
- Contact damage is still a thing in this game, despite how much people pointed out that it sucked in hollow knight. Except this time is way worse because the game is way faster and so are you, so running into the enemy by accident, or the enemy teleporting on top of you, or randomly deciding to jump when you try to pogo, are all massively more likely in this game than it ever was in hollow knight.
- Act 3 feels like a slog. Every enemy gains a MASSIVE pool of HP, to the point that even after upgrading your nail at its maximum possible damage, overworld enemies still feel like HP sponges. And the difficulty spikes massively with the mandatory bosses, to the point they stop feeling like challenges and more like frustrating hurdles to get over with.
- The last Item needed to fully upgrade your nail is locked behind getting a high score in several different minigames you only unlock after rescuing all of this game's equivalent to grubs. The minigames are fine, but locking such a valuable item behind them makes them feel mandatory, which massively diminishes any enjoyment you could've gotten out of them. The minigames would've genuinely been a lot better if the reward was worse or none whatsoever.
- This game contains lots of dead-ends that literally contain nothing, and never contain anything. Only exist to make the map appear larger and waste time. Extremely disappointing whenever I found one.
- Mount fay is an area of the game where its really cold and you take damage if you stay too long on it. And there is nothing in the game that tells you that you have to defy common sense and actually go exploring it while taking constant environmental damage, instead of the logical and intuitive alternative that would've been finding an upgrade that lets you enter the cold area without taking cold area damage, because said item is found at the very END of the cold area.
- The beast crest, one of the equipable movesets that you can learn, is really underpowered despite being fun and unique in concept. A super aggressive moveset that loses the ability to heal on demand for a damage buff that lets you steal health from foes. Sounds awesome until you realize that the life-steal effect is capped at 3 masks only, so at best you're getting just as much healing as usual, and more often than not you're spending exactly as much silk (this game's soul meter) to heal LESS or NOTHING AT ALL if the boss decides to stall out the buff, which happens a lot because the duration is very short and is cut even shorter if you take damage, which you will if you're playing aggressively as the mechanics encourage you to. If that wasn't enough, it also has no blue item slots, which contain 90% of the good passive items that would've synergized excellently with the crest, giving you only two red slots of which there are exactly 2 items that synergize with the crest so there's zero build variety there, and two yellow slots, which contain some of the worst items in the game, to the point that even after you've unlocked every yellow item in the game, sometimes there might be a slot that could just as well be empty because there is nothing useful to put in there that will have an effect whatsoever.
- Overall I just really don't like how hard it is compared to hollow knight. The difficulty in that game was perfectly fine, it didn't need "improving" by making it harder, specially *this* hard. Silksong is a game that demands you grind many hours banging your head against a wall, rather than a smooth sailing main story that slowly ups the difficulty and offers you some optional hard challenges to prove your skill. Silksong completely breaks a perfectly good difficulty curve in favor of unforgiving difficulty; Which admitedly, can be fun, sometimes it was fun, but is not what you would've expected coming fresh from Hollow Knight, and ends up being very jarring.
The game is more interested in testing your patience rather than your skill.

well ok surely that's not a complete deal breaker right? unfortunately it kinda is? remember how i mentioned almost every other crest just feels useless, because this is a big trend in this game, you'll feel weak no matter what, what do i mean by this? lightning round:
-an impressive amount of tools are completely useless, there's no variety to builds as once you have the best stuff that's what you'll use and what everyone else will tell you to use.
-upgrading your needle literally might as well not be a feature since enemies get a secret damage reduction, because why should you ever feel powerful traversing through early areas in a METROIDVANIA.
-defensive upgrades like extra masks or max silk (soul) are so unbelievably far and few between that by the time you get your 7th mask, which is a huge deal when everything does 2 damage you're probably already done with 60% of the game, the 7th mask would be your SECOND HEALTH UPGRADE.

There are a lot of things to love about Silksong. Highly detailed, smartly designed areas, beautiful music, intricate and complex fighting system, the lore that was developed with sincere care, a ton of secrets to explore... So much truly fantastic stuff that was spoiled for me by a stupidly over-the-top difficulty. 

I get it, there are games that are made to challenge players – and I'm not a stranger to loving such projects. Sekiro and Lies of P made me swear and sweat so much that at some moments I wanted to quit them – or smash my gamepad against the wall. Some episodes of Silksong's predecessor, Hollow Knight, were extremely unforgiving and took everything to beat them—such as the White Palace or the Colosseum final stage. But every time my character died in those games I felt that was fair. It was the lack of skills from my side, my impatience, my misunderstanding of games' rules. Those games were very hard – but fair and rewarding. Every victory in them felt well deserved, well timed and brought something cool as a prize – from a new tool to a cool plot turn. 

But Silksong... It is just a challenge after challenge after challenge. Like everything the game designer cared about was how to make player's experience more difficult. Enemies have a ridiculous amount of health, and needle upgrades don't help much — especially in the third act. Most of them are almost unreachable for your attacks, since those are pretty evasive fliers. And there are a lot of them. A LOT: developers are obsessed with locking you in in a small room where you have to fight one wave of enemies after another. Bosses constantly spam their minions, so in addition to dealing with one lethal threat with quirky attack patterns you have to monitor another 2-3 less dangerous enemies, wasting your focus in the process. Using combat tools in such situations sounds like a cool concept, but they require resources to craft — and you'll find that you are out of those pretty soon, and must tediously farm them. Now add the fact that almost everything in this game could kill you in 3-4 touches (hi, dear contact damage), polish it with the lack of checkpoints and the need of going through a boring runback across the half of the map on some bosses. And, finally, put some bugs with controls which aren't very user-friendly from the get-go. Now you see the whole picture.

Silksong is a great game for competitive players whose life is dedicated to gaming, I guess. Unfortunately, I'm not one of them – and can't recommend Silksong to any relatively casual gamer, such as myself. If you are ready to dedicate a huge chunk of your time and energy to master it, and okay with all the pain of this process, you'll be highly rewarded with the things from the first paragraph. Otherwise, just save your money.

Hollow Knight: Silksong is a sequel that I had frankly a lot of expectations for, and if I am honest… This game exceeded all the expectations I had.

[b]Story-wise[/b], one thing I instantly noticed is how much more present the story feels during gameplay. While I’m not entirely sure how to explain it, but the best way I can describe it is that it feels like you always have a certain goal in mind, and that goal constantly shifts as you progress. Now, this is a goal largely set by yourself, so it can be quite personal, but I personally felt like I always had some idea of what I was searching for or what I was working towards. It made the story feel more integrated into the actual gameplay than it did in Hollow Knight. Hornet also feels much more alive as a protagonist. Obviously, a large part of this comes from the fact that she actually speaks, unlike the Knight, but I think there is more to it than that. 

[b]Atmosphere-wise[/b], I think Silksong stands just as tall as Hollow Knight, if not slightly higher. The locations throughout Pharloom feel much more alive, which creates a noticeable contrast with Hollow Knight. In that game, Hallownest was intentionally designed as a fallen and decaying kingdom, so much of its atmosphere revolved around ruin, isolation, and the remnants of a world that had already collapsed. Pharloom, by comparison, feels far more active and inhabited, giving its environments a greater sense of vitality. Detailed background lighting, sharper animations, and a more dynamic audio design all contribute to this. Traversing through Pharloom feels more reactive. These elements make the environments feel more like living spaces that exist independently of the player that it did in Hollow Knight. Personally, I prefer the atmosphere of Silksong over the original, but I think this ultimately comes down to personal preference. The two games are clearly going for different atmospheric identities: Hollow Knight embraces a melancholic, decaying world, while Silksong leans more toward something vibrant, animated, and constantly in motion yet still quite melancholic.

[b]Gameplay-wise[/b], Silksong is a massive step above Hollow Knight for me. Hollow Knight already has incredibly satisfying movement, but the Knight generally feels more grounded. His movement is deliberate, and while abilities such as Mantis Claw, Monarch Wings, and Crystal Dash give him considerable mobility, they often feel more like tools for navigating the world than direct extensions of his combat style. Hornet, by comparison, feels as though her entire moveset has been designed around movement and momentum.
One of the biggest additions in Silksong is the Tool system, which feels far more active and gameplay-focused than Hollow Knight’s Charms. In Hollow Knight, Charms primarily modify the Knight’s existing abilities, affecting things such as damage, spell efficiency, movement, or healing. Tools, by comparison, feel much more like actual pieces of equipment that you actively incorporate into your gameplay. Rather than simply altering how Hornet’s abilities function, they can give her entirely new ways to attack, defend herself, or interact with enemies.
What I particularly appreciate about Tools is how much more connected they make preparation to your actual playstyle. A Tool isn’t simply a passive bonus that you equip and then forget about. Many of them provide abilities that you can deliberately activate during combat, effectively making your equipment another component of your moveset. This creates a much greater distinction between different playstyles, because changing your Tools can fundamentally alter how you approach an encounter rather than simply making the same strategy slightly more effective.
Another particularly interesting addition is the Crest system. Crests essentially function as different loadouts that can fundamentally change the way Hornet plays. Rather than simply providing passive bonuses like Charms, different Crests can alter aspects of her moveset, attacks, and overall combat style.
Then there are Silk Skills. These are special abilities that give Hornet additional ways to utilize her silk during combat. What makes them particularly interesting is how distinct they are from one another, giving you a variety of active abilities that you can incorporate into your playstyle.
Now all I said is mostly scratching the surface of the difference in gameplay and I truly think that gameplay wise, this game is miles better than Hollow Knight

Overall, Hollow Knight: Silksong takes everything that made the original special and expands upon it in meaningful ways. Its story feels more integrated into the gameplay, giving Hornet a stronger sense of purpose as she moves through Pharloom. The atmosphere is just as impressive, trading Hallownest’s decaying isolation for a more vibrant, active, and living world without losing the melancholic ton. Most importantly, the gameplay feels like a major evolution, with Hornet’s movement, Tools, Crests, and Silk Skills creating far more depth and freedom in both exploration and combat.
While Hollow Knight remains an incredible game, Silksong feels like a genuine step forward rather than simply a bigger version of its predecessor. After all the expectations surrounding it, the fact that it managed to exceed mine is genuinely impressive. If you enjoyed Hollow Knight or simply love challenging Metroidvania games, [b]Hollow Knight: Silksong is a must-buy[/b].

This is such a great game in terms of the world, story, visuals, music and gameplay mechanics (and the cost of the game is almost ridiculously low) but it’s massively let down by what I am going to call overly sadistic game design. I almost stopped playing the game completely at one point because I was getting so tired of one punishing challenge after another (honestly think I should have just dropped it there for good). I actually said out loud "I do not play video games to feel this frustrated." Worth noting I'm not a slouch when it comes to games, I've beaten plenty of hard ones.

I cannot in good faith recommend this game to most players as this feels tailored towards the elitists who loved the hardest and most punishing challenges in the original HK and wanted basically an entire game's worth of that. In the original the especially hard parts were largely optional whereas here it’s the entire game - it's unrelenting and I felt exhausted by the end of it. I also think the way in which the game is hard feels very unrewarding:
[list]
[*]Regular enemies are annoying - they have bloated HP and too many deal double damage.
[*]Flying enemy AI is beyond frustrating - they always hover just out of reach and pelt you with projectiles.
[*]Too many hazards deal double damage - it’s overly punishing.
[*]No contact damage with a stationary enemy should do double damage.
[*]Too many platforming sections have annoying flying enemies midway through who will almost inevitably hit you while you are trying to navigate the platforming.
[*]Far too many bosses have regular enemy gauntlets before them. Rather than this be a rare occurrence that fits thematically, it feels like most of the time. It’s just tedious.
[*]Too many bosses also swarm you with regular enemies and at times you can have almost literally nowhere to go without getting hit if the enemy AI moves in a certain way.
[*]Bosses have too much HP and become an endurance test unless you start utilising most likely one of a few handful of tactics to eat away at their health (I'm looking at you cogflies, tacks and poison).
[*]Shard and tool balance is off. I think ideally the game would just be better if you could use your tools to their limits after every bench rest without any shard economy at all, as it can lead to mind-numbing grinding if you use your tools on a boss too many times and fail. And using tools on the bosses feels mandatory when they start getting harder. The additional allowance in tool use could make fighting regular enemies less frustrating as well.
[*]Some rewards were really underwhelming, consisting of a few beads or shards that were pitiful in quantity.
[*]I felt like maxing out everything in prep for the final bosses / final boss was mandatory rather than optional, especially given some of the above points.
[/list]
Team Cherry - I think you came extremely close to making an amazing game but lost sight of what is fun and enjoyable. I could happily replay the original HK any time, but I won’t be touching Silksong with a barge pole unless you make serious changes to the difficulty (just add a separate "hard mode" for the elitists keeping it as-is).

This game is pretty good, but disappointing compared to Hollow Knight. I adore Hollow Knight but Silksong is a mixed bag. 

Enemies are almost unilaterally more tanky, so fighting them often becomes a chore, even after damage upgrades. They also often feel far cheaper, because they have more erratic movesets, so engaging with them feels more random and the insane frequency of two mask damage is stupid. In the original, that was reserved for major bosses and stuff like that and there you became far tankier far more quickly. 

It ends up that most of the time, enemies you're fighting literally take more hits than the player, even when the screen is full of them. So you are a 2-3 hit glass cannon, except you're not a cannon, you're a peashooter. 

More of the encounters also feel cheap. Several "lock doors till you kill all the waves" feel half luck-based with how the several enemies choose to attack. In other places, darkness makes it so enemies jump in from out of view, making it almost impossible to avoid the enemy except by tedious baiting. 

Bosses also feel pretty tanky, which means the fights often end up becoming more about endurance, which feels worse. 

In short, it is far harder to avoid damage, because enemy movesets are far more erratic and with shorter tells and most things feel more random. This is made worse by the way the basic attacks also seem to have far shorter range. It also kinda feels like the hitboxes of player and enemies are too large, to the detriment of the player, so that being within attack range is almost always a hair's breadth from collision damage. 

The reduced freedom in how to use charms is also a letdown, particularly when they are mostly so insignificant that the "balance" of charm types feel pointless. 

The items are the only innovation I like, as well as the varied movesets. 

Overall, the game is a very mixed experience for me. The style, story and atmosphere are all great. I want to keep playing and there is a lot to like. But it feels far more unfair, in a bad way, more luck-based. Not helped by how, with such high damage from everything, you barely get the chance to learn enemy movesets before you die. Particularly because the movement feels less controlled.

Honestly, it feels like the developers lost sight of what a good progression is and what a good balance between player and enemy power is. Ultimately, it almost feels like they were more interested in making "super-hard game for hardcore players" instead of something polished and fair. 

I really hope they tweak it. In Hollow Knight I would sometimes go "Gah, dang!" when something went wrong, but then think "OK, fair". 

In this game, I find myself way too often going "oh, come on, that's just stupid and random." 

I've never felt compelled to review a game before, but this got me over the edge. I want to love this game, but in most ways, I'd call it worse than Hollow Knight. So Silksong gets a like but honestly not a recommendation.

I am left with ironically a HOLLOW feeling inside of me that I wasted 90 hrs on a game that wanted me to fail and in the end, I did fail to complete Act 3. In the end, Silksong made me feel hollow inside and made me think I wasted 90 hrs on something that was designed to make me fail anyways. Nearly every enemy in Hollow Knight drops geo regardless of circumstance (except in the colosseum but you get payed at the end anyways), geo at most bounces a few times on the ground and it doesn't break on spikes meaning you can pick it up with the Gathering Swarm charm.

Silksong on the other hand decides that only enemies that would carry rosaries for lore will drop them on death. Enemies that would drop rosaries don't if you're fighting them in an "arena" setting. Rosaries bounce AND ROLL on top of breaking on spikes (and their equivalents throughout the various areas in the game) meaning that the main use for the magnet tool is to save time picking them up and/or saving any rosaries on the brink of destruction.

I can also bring up how many enemies do more damage with the relative same amount of health to hollow knight meaning that it's more likely you'll lose your rosaries in Silksong from dying. But I want to put articulate that, as someone who played Steel soul mode to 100% and then some, that my issue is not how hard it is to keep rosaries because of a skill issue. Rather, my problem is that I would rather not have to grind out the remaining amount of rosaries I need for buying both necessary (for completion) and accessory items and that I believe the combination of all the factors I list above is the primary culprit for making acquiring them more of a chore than it has to be. 

I'd be extremely curious to see how many rosaries are lost in a given playthrough due to them breaking and/or how many would be gained if enemies that are supposed to have rosaries always dropped them.

I am 40+ hours into Silksong, and while I genuinely love the atmosphere, the characters, and the sense of discovery, I am experiencing more frustration than joy. It is a stunning game, like it's predecessor, which I really loved 10/10, I feel Silksong is bogged down by mechanical "friction" that feels like it was designed purely to annoy the player rather than provide a fair challenge.

The main issues:

Cheap Contact Damage: Simply touching an enemy—even if they aren’t attacking—costs you 2 or 3 masks. Because Hornet is tall, the tips of her ears often clip an enemy's hitbox. It feels terrible to be penalized so heavily for a pixel-perfect error while enemies feel like poise-heavy tanks.

Input Conflicts: Mapping the Special Move (Silk) and Tools to the same button (RB) is a baffling UX choice. In high-stress fights, it is far too easy to mis-input a tool and accidentally waste the Silk you desperately needed for healing.

The "Parachute" Dress: The flutter mechanic is way too sensitive. It frequently activates when I’m just trying to tap-jump, killing my momentum and floating me directly into hazards or enemies.

Mechanical Inconsistency: Ledge grabs are unreliable compared to the first game, and the constant "pogo" parkour feels like a tedious chore rather than a rewarding test of skill.

My Advice to New Players, specially if you are a casual gamer:
The world is worth seeing, but the "cheap ♥♥♥♥" in the base game can be soul-crushing. Ive never used mods in a single player game, not even with Silksong, but for new players I highly recommend looking into the modding community, maybe with mods your experience could be better than mine.

Final Verdict: Good game, beautiful art, 
but questionable design. Feels designed to be frustrating instead of joyful. I can only recommend this to hardcore players and for players who want to see more of Hollow Knight world, but if you are just new... then forget about this ♥♥♥♥ and buy Elden Ring or something else.

[h2]TL;DR: Great game, worse Hollow Knight. 8/10[/h2]

For context: the original Hollow Knight is my favorite game of all time. I've beaten it deathless and without upgrading my character. So when I say Silksong frustrated me, it's not a skill issue rant.

If Hollow Knight gives you a wall and tells you to go find a pickaxe, Silksong expects you to break through it with your head.

[h2]The good[/h2]
[list]
[*] [b]Movement is god-tier.[/b] Hornet glides through levels like a ballerina. Traversal is so fluid it's basically its own form of fun, so the huge map never feels like a chore to cross.
[*] [b]Combat has depth.[/b] Pogo, parries, deflecting projectiles, tools (spears, knives, potions, grenades), and Crests that completely change your moveset or healing. You can build a mage, a tool spammer, whatever you want.
[*] [b]Exploring new areas[/b] is the best part. Almost every biome brings new enemies, mechanics and upgrades. Greymoor, Shellwood, Deep Docks and the Citadel are phenomenal, classic Metroidvania design.
[*] [b]Art and music are stunning.[/b] Tons of tiny details, multilayered backgrounds, and another incredible Christopher Larkin soundtrack.
[*] [b]Story and lore[/b] are coherent and well thought out, and Hornet actually talking makes the narrative much easier to follow.
[/list]

[h2]The bad[/h2]
[list]
[*] [b]Less Metroidvania, more Souls.[/b] Many areas are fairly linear with shortcuts. You clear them on the first pass and never come back. Backtracking often leads to a room with a handful of rosaries.
[*] [b]Some secrets are absurdly hidden[/b], Dark Souls illusory wall style. Good luck getting 100% without a guide.
[*] [b]The balance feels like a stream challenge run.[/b] HK's endgame damage (2 masks per hit) becomes the default a few hours in, while your HP stays at base level. Getting knocked into spikes by a boss can take 4 masks in a second. The new healing (3 masks at once, but only with full silk) is the only thing that makes this work. If you get chunked with no silk, you need 9 hits on 1 HP to heal.
[*] [b]Stingy direct progression.[/b] Twice as many silk upgrades as HK for the same endpoint. Your first needle upgrade is basically it until Act 2. One extra mask barely matters when you die in 3 hits anyway.
[*] [b]"Rage-game" design.[/b] A bench that's a trap (the only one in the whole game, using the same assets), a boss that explodes on death and nearly one-shots you, flying enemies that fall on you for double damage. Consequences way out of proportion to the mistake.
[*] [b]Gauntlets everywhere.[/b] Locked-arena wave fights every 15 minutes against enemies you've already beaten, often copy-pasted arenas, often with no reward at all (drops disabled). One mandatory 10-wave gauntlet ends in a boss, so every death means 10 more minutes to try again.
[*] [b]Lazy bosses.[/b] Few of them, many with 2 to 4 attacks spammed at high speed and high damage. Lots of them spawn random adds, so RNG decides how hard the fight is. Some are recycled up to three times as mandatory fights.
[*] [b]Broken economy.[/b] Paid benches are fine (rosary strings exist for that), but shop prices are huge and about half the enemies drop nothing. You WILL farm rosaries, and shell shards too if you rely on tools.
[b]Little to no rewards.[/b] Many bosses give nothing, one 30-minute area gives you... a Steam achievement. Clearing a zone for an hour gets you 30 rosaries. For a game with speedrun and deathless achievements, this kills replay value.
[*] [b]Quests[/b] are MMO-style fetch/kill tasks, a leftover from when Silksong was a DLC, and they're mandatory to reach the endgame. Courier quests are basically mini platforming Death Stranding: you'll either love them or hate them.
[*] [b]Minor bugs[/b]: bosses vanishing between phases and just dying, broken scripts, inconsistent hitboxes. Rare, and the devs are patching quickly.
[/list]

[h2]Act 3 (spoilers)[/h2]
[spoiler]Story-wise it's great fanservice that ties up most threads from HK. Lace's arc feels chaotic and underexplained, and Grandmother Silk appears in like two scenes, so the antagonist never really lands. Gameplay-wise, the jump to the endgame is barely noticeable because the whole game already had endgame balance. Most side bosses give nothing or near-useless items. And the final boss of a multi-dozen-hour game is... a third Lace fight with extra AoE attacks, partly recycled from other enemies. Seriously? The whole act feels rushed and done on the cheap: barely any new areas, recycled enemies, and the difficulty bump is just the same modifiers slapped on everything.[/spoiler]

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
The core gameplay is impeccable, and most of the problems show up only when you dig into the details, so you might not even notice them. This is for HK veterans who want a bigger challenge and Souls fans who like platformers. If you're new to hard games, it might break you.
